units.title: Making decisions
units.summary: Relational and logical operators, if, if/else, nested and chained decisions, flags, string and char comparison, the conditional operator, switch, and variable scope.

lessons.title: Relational operators and the if statement
lessons.html:
The idea: a program that can choose

So far every program has run each statement once, top to bottom. Real programs must choose. A bank program should print a warning only when the balance is below zero. To choose, the program asks a yes-or-no question about its data, "is the balance less than 0?", and the answer decides what runs next. This lesson covers how to ask the question (a comparison) and how to act on the answer (the if statement).

Relational operators: asking the question

A relational operator compares two values. The name comes from what it tests: how the two values relate. C++ has six. The examples use a = 5 and b = 8.

OperatorMeaningExampleResult
>greater thana > bfalse
<less thana < btrue
>=greater than or equal toa >= 5true
<=less than or equal tob <= 7false
==equal toa == 5true
!=not equal toa != btrue

A comparison written with one of these operators, such as a < b, is called a relational expression. Its value is always true or false, so it is also called a Boolean expression. If you know Python, the six operators are spelled exactly as in Python.

Spelling rules. The two-character operators have no space inside them. When an operator contains =, the = comes second: <=, >=, !=. Say the words to remember the order: "less than, or equal to" puts the < first. The ! means "not", so != reads "not equal". These are not C++ operators and do not compile: =<, =>, <> (not equal in some other languages, such as SQL) and !== (from JavaScript).

What a comparison produces: true or false, shown as 1 or 0

Every relational expression has a value, and that value is a bool: true or false. When C++ prints a bool, or uses one in arithmetic, true becomes the number 1 and false becomes 0. So by default cout shows digits, not words.

int a = 5, b = 8;
cout << (a < b) << endl;    // 1   5 is less than 8
cout << (a > b) << endl;    // 0   5 is not greater than 8
cout << (a == 5) << endl;   // 1
cout << (9 < 4) << endl;    // 0

Python prints True and False. C++ prints the digit. So "the value of 9 < 4" is 0.

To see the words instead, send boolalpha to cout. It stays switched on for everything printed after it.

bool ok = (3 != 4);                // ok holds true
cout << ok << endl;                // 1
cout << boolalpha << ok << endl;   // true
cout << (2 > 9) << endl;           // false

Why the parentheses? C++ does << before < or >, so cout << 7 > 2; means (cout << 7) > 2, which does not compile. Put a comparison in parentheses when you print it.

Order of operations

Precedence is the rule for which operator is worked out first when an expression has several. For the operators so far the order is:

  1. Arithmetic: * / %, then + -.
  2. The four size comparisons: < > <= >=.
  3. The two equality tests: == !=.
  4. Assignment: =.

Operators on the same level are worked left to right. Here is a worked example with x = 3 and y = 7:

x + 4 == y       x + 4 is 7, then 7 == 7        value 1
y - x > x * 2    4 > 6                         value 0
1 == 4 > 2       level 2 first: 4 > 2 is true, 1
                 then level 3: 1 == 1          value 1

Look at the last line. Working left to right would do 1 == 4 (0), then 0 > 2 (0), and give 0. That is wrong. The size comparison goes first because it sits higher in the list.

C++ has no chained comparisons

In math, and in Python, 0 <= x <= 100 means "x is between 0 and 100". In C++ it does not. Both operators are on the same level, so C++ works left to right: (0 <= x) <= 100. The first comparison gives 1 or 0, and then that 1 or 0 is compared with 100.

int x = 500;
0 <= x <= 100
step 1:  0 <= 500     true, so 1
step 2:  1 <= 100     true, so 1
result:  true, although 500 is not between 0 and 100

Whatever x is, step 1 gives 0 or 1, both are less than 100, so the test is always true. x > 5 > 2 fails the other way: step 1 gives 0 or 1, neither is greater than 2, so it is always false. Both compile. The compiler may warn, but the program runs and gives the wrong answer. The correct range test joins two comparisons with the "and" operator &&, covered in the logical operators lesson of this unit.

The opposite of a comparison

The opposite (or negation) of a test is true exactly when the test is false. Either a is less than b, or it is not, and "not less than" means "greater than or equal to". So the opposite of a < b is a >= b. The "or equal" moves across, because the case where the two are equal must land on exactly one side.

TestOppositeSame test, sides swapped
a < ba >= bb > a
a > ba <= bb < a
a <= ba > bb >= a
a == ba != bb == a

Swapping the sides does not give the opposite. It gives the same test written backwards: a < b and b > a always agree, just as "Ann is shorter than Bo" means "Bo is taller than Ann". The trap is mixing the two ideas. Compare p < q with q >= p when both are 4: 4 < 4 is false, but 4 >= 4 is true. To check whether two tests match, always try equal values.

The if statement: acting on the answer

The if statement runs a statement only when a condition is true. The condition is the expression inside the parentheses.

if (condition)
    statement;

If the condition is true, the statement runs. If it is false, the statement is skipped. Either way, the program then carries on with whatever comes next. The statement under the if is conditionally executed: it runs only under that condition. The if is the simplest decision structure, also called a selection structure.

int balance;
cin >> balance;
if (balance < 0)
    cout << "Overdrawn" << endl;
cout << "Done" << endl;
User typesbalance < 0Output
-20trueOverdrawn, then Done
50falseDone

Done prints both times because it is not part of the if. Unlike Python's if balance < 0:, C++ needs parentheses around the condition, has no colon, and ignores indentation. That last point matters below.

In a flowchart, an if is a diamond holding the condition. The "yes" arrow passes through the conditionally executed statement, the "no" arrow goes around it, and the two meet again below. In pseudocode: If balance < 0 Then, the action, End If.

A first look at else, which the next lesson covers fully: an if can be followed by else and a second statement that runs only when the condition is false. Exactly one of the two runs.

if (balance < 0)
    cout << "Overdrawn";
else
    cout << "OK";        // runs when balance < 0 is false

Any number can be a condition

A condition does not have to be a comparison. C++ accepts any number and uses one rule: 0 is false, and every other value is true, negative numbers included.

int items = -2;
if (items)
    cout << "not zero" << endl;      // runs: -2 is not 0
if (0)
    cout << "never printed" << endl;

That rule is behind the first trap.

Trap 1: = is not ==

One = is assignment: it stores a value. Two, ==, is comparison: it asks a question. Mixing them up still compiles.

int count = 0;
if (count = 3)
    cout << "three" << endl;
cout << count << endl;

Trace it:

count = 3     stores 3 in count. An assignment
              also has a value: the value stored, 3
if (3)        3 is not 0, so the condition is true
output:       three
              3

The test was meant to ask "is count equal to 3?". Instead it changed count and was true every time. if (count = 0) is the reverse: it stores 0, and 0 is false, so its statement never runs. Python rejects if count = 3:. C++ accepts it and at most warns.

Trap 2: a semicolon after the condition

int temp = 50;
if (temp > 90);
    cout << "Hot day" << endl;

This prints Hot day, though 50 is not greater than 90. A semicolon on its own is a complete statement that does nothing, called a null statement (or empty statement). The if controls the one statement right after its parentheses, and here that is the lone ;. So the if decides whether to do nothing, and the cout is an ordinary statement that always runs. It compiles without error.

Trap 3: without braces, an if controls one statement

int score = 40;
if (score >= 60)
    cout << "Pass" << endl;
    cout << "Certificate sent" << endl;

The indentation suggests both lines belong to the if. The compiler ignores indentation. Without braces an if controls exactly one statement, the first one after the condition. Here the condition is false, so Pass is skipped, and Certificate sent prints anyway.

To make several statements depend on the condition, put them in braces. Statements inside { } form a block, and the if treats the whole block as its one statement.

if (score >= 60)
{
    cout << "Pass" << endl;
    cout << "Certificate sent" << endl;
}

Now both lines are skipped when the score is 40. Many programmers use braces even around one statement, so that adding a line later cannot cause this bug. Still indent the controlled statements: people read indentation even though the compiler does not.

Mistakes students make

  • Writing =< or =>. The = goes second: <=, >=.
  • Using <> or !== for not equal. C++ uses !=.
  • Expecting cout to print true or false. It prints 1 or 0 unless boolalpha was sent first.
  • Writing 0 <= x <= 100 or x > 5 > 2 as in math.
  • Working left to right when == sits next to < or >. The size comparison goes first.
  • Swapping the sides of a < b to get its opposite. b > a is the same test. The opposite is a >= b.
  • Writing if (x = 5) for if (x == 5). It changes x and is always true.
  • Putting a semicolon after if (...), so the next statement always runs.
  • Trusting indentation. Without braces only the first statement belongs to the if.

What to remember for the test

  • The six relational operators: > < >= <= == !=. A comparison made with one is a relational (or Boolean) expression. Its value is true or false, printed as 1 or 0.
  • Order: arithmetic, then < > <= >=, then == !=, then =. Same level: left to right.
  • As a condition, 0 is false and any other value is true.
  • The opposite of < is >=, of > is <=, of == is !=. Swapping the sides keeps the same meaning.
  • if (condition) statement; needs the parentheses, has no semicolon after them, and controls one statement or one braced block.
  • For a "what does this print" question, work each condition out to 1 or 0, then follow which statements run.

lessons.title: Expanding the if: if/else, nesting and floating-point
lessons.html:
The idea: two roads, exactly one is taken

A plain if answers one question: do this, or skip it. Often a program needs to do one thing when the answer is yes and a different thing when it is no. A cinema charges 6 dollars for anyone 65 or older and 9 dollars for everyone else. That is the if/else statement.

if (age >= 65)
    price = 6;
else
    price = 9;
ageage >= 65What runsprice after
70truethe if part6
65truethe if part6
30falsethe else part9

Hold this picture: the condition is a fork in the road. The program goes down exactly one branch, never both and never neither, and then the two roads meet and the program carries on after the whole statement.

  • The else has no condition of its own. It simply means "otherwise".
  • It works like Python's else:, but with no colon. The condition still needs its parentheses.
  • The condition follows the same rule as before: 0 is false, anything else is true. With int n = 0;, if (n) is false, so the else part runs.

Blocks: more than one statement on a branch

Each branch controls one statement. To put several statements on a branch, wrap them in curly braces { }. The braces and everything inside them form a block (also called a compound statement), and C++ treats the whole block as one statement. No semicolon is needed after a closing brace.

if (hours > 40)
{
    overtime = hours - 40;
    pay = 40 * rate + overtime * rate * 1.5;
}
else
{
    pay = hours * rate;
}

The compiler decides what belongs to a branch from the braces only. It ignores indentation completely. Programmers indent the statements inside a branch so that people can see the structure, but indenting a line does not put it inside the if. This is the opposite of Python, where indentation is the structure.

Missing braces without an else. The second statement is ordinary code that always runs:

int n = -3;
if (n > 0)
    cout << "A";
    cout << "B";      // not part of the if: prints B

Missing braces with an else. Now the code does not even compile:

if (qty == 0)
    cout << "Empty. ";
    cout << "Reorder.";   // ordinary statement: the if has ended
else                       // error: else without a previous if
    cout << "OK";

Read it the way the compiler does. The if owns only cout << "Empty. ";. That finishes the if statement. cout << "Reorder."; is a separate statement. An else must come straight after the statement its if controls, so this else has no if to join, and g++ reports "else without a previous if". Braces around the two cout lines fix it.

A stray semicolon causes the same error. In if (sales == 2000); bonus = 50; else bonus = 0; the lone ; is a null statement (a statement that does nothing) and it is all the if controls. bonus = 50; is then ordinary code, and the else is stranded. The same goes for } followed by ; before an else. Without an else, a semicolon after the condition is not an error: it compiles, the if controls nothing, and the next line always runs. That silence is what makes it dangerous.

Watch the equals signs. The condition compares with ==. The branches store with =. bonus == 50; on a branch compiles but only asks a question and throws the answer away, so bonus never changes.

Nested if statements

A branch can contain any statement, including another if. An if inside another if or else is a nested if. Use one when a second question only makes sense after the first has been answered.

if (n > 0)
{
    cout << "positive ";
    if (n % 2 == 0)
        cout << "even";
    else
        cout << "odd";
}
else
    cout << "not positive";

Recall that % gives the remainder after division: 25 % 2 is 1, 8 % 2 is 0. A number is even when n % 2 == 0.

nn > 0n % 2 == 0Output
25true1 == 0, falsepositive odd
8true0 == 0, truepositive even
-4falsenever testednot positive

The key fact: an inner if is tested only when the program reaches it. One nested in the if part is tested only when the outer condition is true. One nested in the else part is tested only when the outer condition is false. With n = -4 the even/odd question is never asked. To trace nested code, work from the outside in: decide the outer condition first, skip the whole branch that is not taken, then step into the branch that is.

The dangling else: which if does an else belong to?

When ifs are nested without braces, there can be two ifs and one else. C++ settles it with one rule: an else belongs to the nearest earlier if that does not already have an else, and that if must not be shut away inside a closed pair of braces. Indentation plays no part.

if (temp > 80)
    if (wind > 10)
        cout << "Hot and breezy";
else
    cout << "Not hot";

The else is lined up with the outer if, but the nearest if is if (wind > 10), so that is its partner. The code really means:

if (temp > 80)
{
    if (wind > 10)
        cout << "Hot and breezy";
    else
        cout << "Not hot";
}
temp, windWhat happensOutput
50, 20outer false: the whole inner if/else is skippednothing
90, 5outer true, inner false: the else runsNot hot (wrong!)
90, 20both trueHot and breezy

To give the else to the outer if, put braces around the inner if. The closing brace ends the inner if, so the else cannot reach in and must take the outer one:

if (temp > 80)
{
    if (wind > 10)
        cout << "Hot and breezy";
}
else
    cout << "Not hot";       // now runs when temp <= 80

Good style avoids the question altogether: use braces on nested ifs and indent each level, so the code looks like what it does.

Decisions in flowcharts

A quick recap of the symbols: an oval marks Start and End, a rectangle (process box) holds a calculation or assignment, a parallelogram holds input or output, and a diamond holds a yes/no question with a Yes exit and a No exit.

  • if with no else: the Yes path goes through the controlled box or boxes, the No path goes through nothing, and the two paths join. A braced block becomes several boxes in a row on the Yes path.
  • if/else: each exit has its own boxes before the join.
  • Nested if: a second diamond sits on one path of the first. A diamond on the Yes path becomes an if inside the if part. On the No path it goes inside the else part.
  • Whatever comes after the whole if statement in the code sits after the join in the chart, so it runs on both paths.

The nested example above as a flowchart: diamond "n > 0?". Yes leads to a box displaying "positive ", then to a second diamond "n % 2 == 0?", whose Yes displays "even" and whose No displays "odd". The first diamond's No displays "not positive". All paths then join. To trace any flowchart, take the current values, answer each diamond's question, and follow only that one arrow.

Comparing floating-point numbers

A double is stored in binary, and most decimal fractions cannot be written exactly in binary. It is the same problem as writing 1/3 in decimal: 0.333333 is close, but it never ends, so any stored copy is slightly off. On a typical PC, which uses the standard IEEE 754 format for double, this happens:

double a = 0.1 + 0.2;
cout << a << endl;            // 0.3   (6 digits hide the error)
cout << (a == 0.3) << endl;   // 0     not equal!
// with setprecision(17):
//   a is   0.30000000000000004
//   0.3 is 0.29999999999999999

The two values differ by about 0.00000000000000006, and == demands an exact match. Python gives the same result: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False there too. So do not test computed floating-point values with == or !=. Two safer approaches:

  • The book's advice: stick to < and > comparisons with floating-point values. if (balance < 0.0) is safe. A tiny error does not change which side of a limit a value is on, except right at the limit.
  • To ask "are these equal?", ask instead "are they close enough?". fabs(x), from <cmath>, gives the absolute value of a double: its size without the sign, so fabs(-2.5) is 2.5. The difference between two values is tiny when its absolute value is below a small tolerance that you choose:
// fabs(a - 0.3) is about 0.00000000000000006
if (fabs(a - 0.3) < 0.000001)
    cout << "close enough";      // this runs

Mistakes students make

  • Trusting indentation. Without braces, a branch is one statement, and the next line is ordinary code.
  • Leaving out braces when a branch has two statements and an else follows. That is a compile error: else without a previous if.
  • Putting a semicolon after if (...). With no else it compiles and the next line always runs. With a statement and then an else after it, it is a compile error.
  • Giving else a condition. It has none: it means "otherwise".
  • Pairing an else with the if it is lined up under. It pairs with the nearest earlier unmatched if not closed off by braces.
  • Testing an inner if when the outer condition sent the program down the other branch.
  • Writing == on a branch that should store a value, or = in a condition that should compare.
  • Comparing computed double values with ==.

What to remember for the test

  • if/else runs exactly one of its two branches, then continues after the whole statement.
  • Each branch is one statement or one braced block. Braces decide the structure, indentation never does.
  • An else must come straight after the statement its if controls, or the code does not compile.
  • A semicolon right after the condition, with no else, is legal: a null statement. It is a logic bug, not a compile error.
  • An inner if is tested only when the program reaches it.
  • Dangling else: an else goes with the nearest earlier if that has no else and is not closed off inside braces.
  • In a flowchart, code after the if statement sits after the paths join and runs on every path.
  • Never use == on computed doubles. Use < and >, or test fabs(a - b) < tolerance.

lessons.title: if/else if chains, initialization and flags
lessons.html:
The idea: one question, many possible answers

An if/else picks one of two roads. Some decisions have more than two. A test score becomes an A, a B, a C or an F. You could do it with nested if/else statements, but each level pushes the code further right and it gets hard to read. C++ offers a flatter way to write the same thing: the if/else if chain (the book calls it the if/else if statement).

if (score >= 90)
    grade = 'A';
else if (score >= 80)
    grade = 'B';
else if (score >= 70)
    grade = 'C';
else
    grade = 'F';

The picture to hold: a row of doors tried from the top down. The program walks to the first door, the first condition. If it is true, the program goes through that door, runs its statement, and leaves the whole chain. It never even looks at the conditions further down. If it is false, the program moves on to the next door. The final else, called the trailing else, is the door at the end that is always open: it runs only when every condition above it was false. If you know Python, else if is C++'s spelling of elif.

Tracing a chain

scoreConditions testedgrade
9595 >= 90 true. Stop.A
8585 >= 90 false, 85 >= 80 true. Stop.B
72false, false, 72 >= 70 true. Stop.C
40false, false, false. The trailing else runs.F

Notice that 95 is also at least 80 and at least 70. It does not matter: the first true condition wins and the rest are skipped. That is why at most one branch of a chain runs. With a trailing else, exactly one runs. Without one, it is possible for nothing to run, when every condition is false.

Order matters

Because the first true condition wins, the order of the tests is part of the logic. Here are the same tests in the wrong order:

if (score >= 70)
    grade = 'C';
else if (score >= 80)
    grade = 'B';
else if (score >= 90)
    grade = 'A';
else
    grade = 'F';

With score = 95, the first test, 95 >= 70, is already true, so the grade is C and the A test is never reached. In fact no score can ever get a B or an A from this code, because anything that is at least 80 is also at least 70 and stops at the first door.

The rule is to test the narrowest case first. With >= tests that means the highest limit first. With < tests it means the lowest limit first:

if (temp < 32)
    cout << "Freezing";
else if (temp < 60)
    cout << "Cold";        // only reached when temp >= 32
else
    cout << "Warm";

By the time the program reaches temp < 60, it already knows temp < 32 was false. So "Cold" means 32 up to 59. To check any chain, pick one value from each range, such as 20, 45 and 75 here, and trace each one.

A chain is a nested if/else in disguise

else if is not a new keyword. It is an else whose one statement happens to be another if. These two pieces of code are exactly the same to the compiler:

if (score >= 90)          if (score >= 90)
    grade = 'A';              grade = 'A';
else if (score >= 80)     else
    grade = 'B';          {
else                          if (score >= 80)
    grade = 'F';                  grade = 'B';
                              else
                                  grade = 'F';
                          }

So every if/else if chain can be rewritten as nested if/else statements, and the other way round. The chain form is preferred only because it is easier to read and does not keep drifting to the right.

A chain versus separate ifs

Separate if statements are independent. Each one is tested, whatever happened before it, so several can run.

// separate ifs                // one chain
if (score >= 90)               if (score >= 90)
    cout << "A";                   cout << "A";
if (score >= 80)               else if (score >= 80)
    cout << "B";                   cout << "B";
if (score >= 70)               else if (score >= 70)
    cout << "C";                   cout << "C";

With score = 95 the separate ifs print ABC, because all three tests are true and nothing stops the later ones. The chain prints A. Use a chain when the cases are mutually exclusive (only one can apply). Use separate ifs when several can apply at once.

Watch where a chain starts. An if that is not preceded by else starts a new statement. In the code below the first if stands alone, and the chain begins at the second if:

int w = 25;
if (w > 20)
    cout << "heavy ";       // separate if: true, prints
if (w > 10)                 // a new chain starts here
    cout << "medium";       // true, prints, chain ends
else
    cout << "light";

Output: heavy medium.

Chains in pseudocode

Pseudocode is plain-language code with no strict rules, used for planning. This course writes actions as Set fee to 5, Add 3 to fee and Display fee, and the chain as If ... Then, Else If ... Then, Else, End If. Trace it exactly like C++: test from the top, run only the first true branch, skip to End If.

Set cost to 5
Set w to 10
If w > 20 Then
    Add 12 to cost
Else If w > 8 Then
    Add 6 to cost
End If
Display cost

Trace: 10 > 20 is false, 10 > 8 is true, so 6 is added and the chain ends. The display shows 11. With w = 3 both tests are false and there is no Else, so nothing is added and it shows 5.

The trailing else is the chain's "none of the above". A switch statement, covered at the end of this unit, has the same idea in its default section.

An if with an initialization clause (C++17)

Since C++17, an if may start with a short definition, then a semicolon, then the condition. The definition is the initialization clause. It is optional: plain if (condition) is still the normal form. A switch accepts the same optional clause.

string name = "Al";
if (int len = name.length(); len < 3)
    cout << "too short";
else
    cout << len << " characters";

Step by step: first the clause runs, so len is created and set to 2. Then the condition len < 3 is tested. It is true, so too short prints. For "Alexandra", len would be 9 and the else would print 9 characters.

Where can len be used? In the condition, the if part and every else part of that statement, and nowhere else. The region of code where a name can be used is called its scope. Once the whole if statement ends, len is gone, and a later cout << len; is a compile error ("not declared in this scope"). In a chain, a variable made in one clause can be used from that clause to the end of the chain, since every later else if sits inside its else part. The point of the clause is to keep a helper variable inside the one decision that needs it.

Flags

A flag is a variable that remembers whether something has happened, so a later part of the program can test it. Think of the little flag on a mailbox: someone raises it when there is mail, and anyone can check it later. A flag is usually a bool, the type that holds only true or false. Older code uses an int holding 0 or 1.

bool discount = false;      // start lowered
if (age >= 65)
    discount = true;        // raise it
if (isStudent)
    discount = true;        // raise it
// ... later ...
if (discount)
    price = price * 0.9;

Three habits matter:

  • Give the flag its starting value when you define it. A local variable (one defined inside a function such as main) that is not given a value does not start at 0 or false. It holds whatever happened to be left in that memory, a garbage value, and reading it is an error in the program.
  • Test a bool directly. if (discount) means the same as if (discount == true) and reads better. Never write if (discount = true): that stores true and is true every time.
  • Use ! for the opposite. ! is the NOT operator: !discount is true when discount is false, and false when it is true. if (!discount) runs when the flag is not set, the same as if (discount == false) or if (discount == 0). The logical operators lesson covers ! fully.

Facts about bool that examiners like:

bool ok = (5 < 2);              // a comparison can be stored: false
cout << ok << " " << !ok;      // prints 0 1
bool b = 25;                    // any nonzero number becomes true
cout << b;                      // prints 1, not 25
bool z = 0;                     // only 0 becomes false

A bool has room for only two values, so storing 25 or -3 keeps just "nonzero", which is true. cout prints it as 1, or as the word true after boolalpha. The keyword is bool. boolean is how Java spells it and is not a C++ type.

Mistakes students make

  • Putting the widest test first, such as score >= 70 before score >= 90, so the later tests can never be reached.
  • Thinking every condition in a chain is tested. Testing stops at the first true one.
  • Thinking the trailing else runs after a branch that matched. It runs only when nothing above matched.
  • Reading a new if as part of the chain above it. Only else if continues a chain.
  • Using separate ifs for exclusive cases, so a value prints several results.
  • Using the initialization variable after the if statement has ended.
  • Leaving a flag or counter without a starting value. A local variable does not start at 0.
  • Writing if (flag = true). Write if (flag).
  • Expecting bool b = 25; to print 25. It prints 1.

What to remember for the test

  • A chain tests top to bottom. The first true condition runs its branch, and the rest are skipped without being tested.
  • The trailing else runs only when every condition above it was false. It is the chain's catch-all, like default in a switch.
  • Order the tests from narrowest to widest: highest limit first for >=, lowest first for <.
  • A chain runs at most one branch. Separate ifs can run several.
  • An if/else if chain is a nested if/else written compactly.
  • if (init; condition) is optional C++17 syntax. The variable lives only inside that if statement and its else parts.
  • A flag is a variable, usually a bool, that records whether something happened. Initialize it, then test it with if (flag) or if (!flag).
  • Any nonzero value stored in a bool becomes true, printed as 1.

lessons.title: Logical operators, ranges, menus and input validation
lessons.html:
The idea: joining small questions into one

Many real decisions depend on more than one fact. "Is the person a teenager?" means "is the age at least 13 and at most 19?". "Is the score invalid?" means "is it below 0 or above 100?". A single comparison cannot say that. A logical operator takes true/false values and combines them, or reverses one, into a single true/false answer. C++ has three:

OperatorNameTrue whenPython
&&ANDboth sides are trueand
||ORat least one side is trueor
!NOTits one operand is false (it flips the value)not

An operand is a value an operator works on. && and || each take two, one on each side. ! takes one, written straight after it. The | character is the vertical bar, usually above the Enter key. Like the comparisons, the result is a bool, so cout prints it as 1 or 0.

Truth tables

A truth table lists every combination of inputs and the result for each. With two inputs there are only four rows, so it is worth knowing them cold.

pqp && qp || q!p
falsefalsefalsefalsetrue
falsetruefalsetruetrue
truefalsefalsetruefalse
truetruetruetruefalse

A quick way to read it: && is false if either side is false. || is true if either side is true. In a program the sides are usually comparisons:

int age = 16;
age >= 13 && age <= 19     // true && true     is true
age < 13 || age > 19       // false || false   is false
!(age >= 18)               // !false           is true

Precedence: which part is worked out first

Here is the order for every operator met so far, from the highest (grouped first) to the lowest:

  1. !
  2. arithmetic: * / %, then + -
  3. < > <= >=
  4. == !=
  5. &&
  6. ||
  7. =

Three consequences that examiners test:

  • Comparisons happen before && and ||, so age >= 13 && age <= 19 needs no extra parentheses. Each comparison becomes true or false, and then they are joined.
  • && comes before ||, just as * comes before +. So a || b && c means a || (b && c). With a true and b, c false, that is true || false, which is true. But (a || b) && c is true && false, which is false. Parentheses change the answer.
  • ! comes before everything else, including comparisons. So !x > 5 means (!x) > 5, not "x is not greater than 5". With x = 3: !3 is !true, which is false (0), and 0 > 5 is false. To negate a comparison, wrap it: !(x > 5). Python is different here: its not x > 5 means not (x > 5).

Associativity is the direction in which operators of the same level are grouped. && and || group left to right, like most operators: a || b || c means (a || b) || c. The ! operator is the exception and groups right to left, so !!x means !(!x). When in doubt, add parentheses. They cost nothing and make the meaning plain.

Short-circuit evaluation

&& and || always work out their left side first. If that already decides the answer, the right side is never evaluated at all. This is called short-circuit evaluation.

  • A && B: if A is false, the result must be false, so B is skipped.
  • A || B: if A is true, the result must be true, so B is skipped.

Skipping B never changes the true/false result. It matters in two situations.

1. It can guard a dangerous step. Dividing by zero is an error.

int count = 0, total = 50;
if (count > 0 && total / count > 10)
    cout << "average above 10";

count > 0 is false, so total / count is never computed and nothing goes wrong. Written the other way round, total / count > 10 && count > 0 would divide by zero before the check. Put the guard on the left.

2. Anything that changes a variable on the right side may not happen. ++n adds 1 to n (the loops unit covers it fully). An assignment such as (y = 10) stores 10 in y. If they sit on a skipped side, they do not run.

int m = 2, n = 7;
bool r = m > 5 && ++n > 0;
step 1:  m > 5 is 2 > 5, false
step 2:  && with a false left side: skip the right
result:  r is false (0), n is still 7

With m < 5 || ++n > 0 the left side is true, so || skips the right side and n again stays 7. Only when the left side does not decide the answer, as in m < 5 && ++n > 0, does ++n run and n becomes 8. Python short-circuits and and or in exactly the same way.

Precedence decides grouping, not which side is looked at first. In a || b && c, precedence groups the pieces as a || (b && c). When the program runs, || still works out its left side, a, first. If a is true, the whole (b && c) part is skipped. For a "what is the value" question this makes no difference: working out b && c first gives the same true/false answer. It matters only when the skipped part would change a variable:

int m = 2, n = 7;
bool r = m < 5 || ++n > 0 && n < 5;
groups as:  m < 5 || (++n > 0 && n < 5)
step 1:     m < 5 is 2 < 5, true
step 2:     || with a true left side: skip the right
result:     r is true (1), n is still 7

Checking ranges

Lesson 1 showed that a chained test such as 13 <= age <= 19 does not work in C++. A range test needs two comparisons and a logical operator.

  • Inside a range: the value must pass both limits, so use &&: age >= 13 && age <= 19.
  • Outside a range: the value fails at least one limit, so use ||: age < 13 || age > 19.

Mixing them up gives a test that is always or never true:

Test121620Verdict
age >= 13 && age <= 19010correct inside test
age < 13 || age > 19101correct outside test
age >= 13 || age <= 19111always true: every number passes one side
age < 13 && age > 19000never true: no number is below 13 and above 19

Translate the words carefully. "At least 13" is >= 13. "At most 19" is <= 19. "More than" is > and "fewer than" or "under" is <. "13 through 19" includes both ends. Writing age > 13 && age < 19 wrongly rejects 13 and 19. Always test the two end values when you check a range.

De Morgan's laws: pushing a NOT inside

Sometimes you have "not (this or that)" and need it without the outer NOT. Think in plain words. "It is not true that it is cold or raining" means "it is not cold, and it is not raining". "It is not true that it is cold and raining" means "it is not cold, or it is not raining". These are De Morgan's laws:

!(A || B)   is the same as   !A && !B
!(A && B)   is the same as   !A || !B

To push a NOT inside, do two things: flip the joining operator (|| becomes &&, or the reverse) and replace each comparison with its opposite (the opposite of < is >=, the opposite of > is <=, as in lesson 1).

!(age < 18 || age > 65)
flip || to &&:          !(age < 18) && !(age > 65)
opposite of each:       age >= 18 && age <= 65

Both say "age is from 18 to 65". A common slip is to flip only one of the two things, or to use > instead of >= for the opposite of <.

Menus

A menu-driven program shows a numbered list of choices, reads the user's choice, and runs the matching code. An if/else if chain (or the switch statement covered later in this unit) does the matching. The final else catches any number that is not on the menu.

int choice;
cout << "1) Add  2) Delete  3) Quit" << endl;
cin >> choice;
if (choice == 1)
    cout << "Adding";
else if (choice == 2)
    cout << "Deleting";
else if (choice == 3)
    cout << "Goodbye";
else
    cout << "Invalid choice";   // 0, 7, -5 ... all land here

Never assume the user will type only what the menu lists. People mistype.

Input validation

Input validation means checking input before using it. The saying is garbage in, garbage out (GIGO): a program that accepts an age of -4 or a menu choice of 9 produces nonsense, however correct its calculations are. The usual pattern is to test for bad input first, with an "outside the range" test, and do the real work only in the else part:

if (choice < 1 || choice > 3)
    cout << "Invalid choice";
else if (choice == 3)
    cout << "Goodbye";
else
    cout << "Working";

If the user types 0, 0 < 1 is true, so || is true at once, "Invalid choice" prints, and the rest of the chain is skipped. Check the boundaries the problem allows: is 0 a legal value? Is 100? That decides between < and <=.

Mistakes students make

  • Writing 1 <= x <= 10. Use x >= 1 && x <= 10.
  • Using || for an inside test, which is always true, or && for an outside test, which is never true.
  • Working a || b && c left to right. && groups first: a || (b && c).
  • Thinking precedence makes the && part run first. It only decides the grouping. || still looks at its left side first and may skip the rest.
  • Reading !x > 5 as "not greater than 5". The ! applies to x alone.
  • Expecting a ++ or an assignment on the right of && or || to run when the left side already decided the answer.
  • Thinking short-circuiting can change the true/false result. It only skips work.
  • Pushing a NOT inside but forgetting to flip && and ||, or getting the opposite of < wrong.
  • Using > and < for "at least" and "at most", which drops the end values.
  • Leaving out the final else in a menu.

What to remember for the test

  • && (AND): true only when both sides are true. || (OR): true when at least one side is true. ! (NOT): flips true and false.
  • Precedence, high to low: !, arithmetic, < > <= >=, == !=, &&, ||, =. So || is the lowest of the logical and comparison operators.
  • && and || group left to right. ! groups right to left.
  • Short circuit: && skips its right side when the left is false. || skips its right side when the left is true.
  • Inside a range: &&. Outside a range: ||.
  • De Morgan: !(A || B) is !A && !B, and !(A && B) is !A || !B.
  • Input validation: test the input before using it, and give menus a final else for invalid choices.

lessons.title: Comparing characters and strings; the conditional operator
lessons.html:
The idea: characters are numbers in disguise

A char does not store a picture of a letter. It stores a small whole number, the character's code, and the computer looks up which symbol that number stands for. The standard table of codes is ASCII. When you compare two characters with <, == or any other relational operator, C++ compares their codes. Once you hold that picture, every rule in the first half of this lesson follows from it. (Python hides the codes behind ord(). In C++ a char already is the number.)

You do not need the whole ASCII table. You need these anchors and the order of the groups:

CharactersCodes
space32
'0' to '9'48 to 57
'A' to 'Z'65 to 90
'a' to 'z'97 to 122

Inside each group the codes run in order with no gaps, so 'A' < 'B' and '3' < '7', as you would expect. The surprises come from the order of the groups: digits come before uppercase letters, and every uppercase letter comes before every lowercase letter.

cout << ('B' < 'a');   // 1   66 < 97: uppercase before lowercase
cout << ('b' < 'B');   // 0   98 < 66 is false
cout << ('5' < 'A');   // 1   53 < 65: digits before letters

So 'Z' < 'a' is true, although Z is the last letter of the alphabet. Upper and lower case versions of the same letter are different characters: 'a' == 'A' is false.

Arithmetic on characters. Because a char is a number, you can add to it. The result of 'c' + 1 is the int 100, and cout prints 100. To get a character back, convert it: char('c' + 1) is 'd'.

Digit characters are not numbers

The character '7', with quotes, is the symbol you see on the key. Its code is 55. The number 7, without quotes, is just seven. They are different values:

'4' == 4      52 == 4     false
'4' == 52     52 == 52    true
'4' - '0'     52 - 48     4

The last line is a standard trick. The digit codes are in order, so subtracting the code of '0' turns any digit character into the number it shows: '8' - '0' is 8.

The same fact gives the test for "is this character a digit?". Since the codes run in order, it is a range test, with quotes on both limits:

if (ch >= '0' && ch <= '9')     // codes 48 to 57
    cout << "digit";

Without the quotes, ch >= 0 && ch <= 9 tests codes 0 to 9. Those are invisible control characters, not digits, so the test is wrong for every real digit. And the usual range traps from the logical operators lesson apply: '0' <= ch <= '9' and ch >= '0' || ch <= '9' are both true for every character.

Comparing strings

The relational operators also work on string objects (with #include <string>). Two strings are compared the way a dictionary orders words, but using character codes instead of the alphabet:

  1. Compare the first characters. If they differ, the string whose character has the smaller code is less. Stop.
  2. If they are the same, move on to the next pair and repeat.
  3. If one string runs out while all its characters have matched, the shorter one is less.
"apple" vs "apricot"
a = a, p = p, then p (112) vs r (114): p is smaller
so "apple" < "apricot"

"sun" vs "sunday"
s = s, u = u, n = n, then "sun" runs out
so "sun" < "sunday"

"Bob" vs "adam"
B (66) vs a (97): B is smaller, stop at once
so "Bob" < "adam"

The last example shows that string comparison is case sensitive. Every uppercase letter is less than every lowercase letter, so any word starting with a capital comes before any word starting with a small letter. It also means == is true only when every character matches, case included: "Cat" == "cat" is false.

Strings of digits are compared as text, not as numbers.

string a = "9", b = "10";
// first characters: '9' (57) vs '1' (49)
// '1' is smaller, so b is less
cout << (a > b);     // 1: "9" comes after "10"

The comparison never looks at how long the numbers are. It stops at the first character that differs. Python strings compare the same way: "Bob" < "adam" and "10" < "9" are both true there too.

One caution. At least one side must be a string object, as in name == "Ann" where name is a string. Two quoted literals, such as "cat" == "cat", are not compared as text. C++ compares where they are stored in memory, so the result cannot be trusted.

The conditional operator ?:

Often an if/else exists only to choose between two values:

if (age < 12)
    fee = 5;
else
    fee = 10;

The conditional operator says the same thing in one expression:

fee = (age < 12) ? 5 : 10;

Read it as a question: "is age under 12? If yes, 5. If no, 10." The form is

condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse

The ? comes right after the condition, and the : separates the two values. It is the only C++ operator with three operands, so it is also called the ternary operator. Python writes the same idea as 5 if age < 12 else 10, with the condition in the middle. C++ puts the condition first.

ageage < 12Value chosenfee
8truethe one after ?5
12falsethe one after :10
30falsethe one after :10

The key difference from if/else: ?: is an expression, something that produces a value, while if/else is a statement that runs code. So you can use ?: anywhere a value fits: on the right of =, or inside a cout.

int larger = (a > b) ? a : b;    // the bigger of a and b
cout << items << (items == 1 ? " item" : " items");

With items equal to 1 the second line prints 1 item, and with 3 it prints 3 items.

Rules to know:

  • Its precedence is very low. It is done after arithmetic, comparisons, &&, || and <<. In int v = x > 2 ? x * 2 : x / 2; the parentheses are not needed: x > 2 is the condition, and the chosen value is stored in v. Inside a cout chain, though, you must wrap the whole thing in parentheses. cout << n % 2 == 0 ? "even" : "odd"; does not compile, because << grabs n % 2 first.
  • Only the chosen value is worked out. avg = (count != 0) ? total / count : 0; never divides when count is 0.
  • Both values should be the same kind: two numbers, or two pieces of text. cond ? "odd" : 1 does not compile.
  • Use it for short choices of a value. When each branch does real work, an if/else is clearer.

Mistakes students make

  • Assuming 'a' < 'B' because a comes first in the alphabet. Uppercase codes are smaller, so 'B' < 'a'.
  • Comparing a digit character with a number: '7' == 7 is false. Use '7' - '0' to get 7.
  • Writing the digit test without quotes: ch >= 0 && ch <= 9.
  • Comparing number strings as numbers. "100" < "25" is true as text.
  • Thinking the shorter string is always less. Length matters only when one string is the start of the other.
  • Forgetting that == on strings is case sensitive.
  • Swapping the two values of ?:. The value for true comes first, right after the ?.
  • Writing : before ?, or a comma instead of :.
  • Leaving out the parentheses around ?: inside a cout.

What to remember for the test

  • Characters compare by code: '0' to '9' are 48 to 57, 'A' to 'Z' are 65 to 90, 'a' to 'z' are 97 to 122. Digits, then uppercase, then lowercase.
  • '7' is the code 55, not 7. '7' - '0' is 7.
  • Digit test: ch >= '0' && ch <= '9'.
  • Strings compare character by character from the left, by code. First difference decides. If one runs out first, it is less. Case matters.
  • cond ? a : b is an expression: a if the condition is true, b if it is false. It is the conditional (ternary) operator, the only one with three operands.
  • Put ?: in parentheses inside a cout.
  • For a character or string question, write down the codes and compare them one position at a time.

lessons.title: The switch statement, initialization and variable scope
lessons.html:
The idea: jump straight to the matching label

Menus and codes lead to chains like if (choice == 1) ... else if (choice == 2) ... else if (choice == 3) ...: one variable compared with == against a list of fixed values. The switch statement is built for exactly that shape.

switch (grade)               // grade is a char
{
    case 'A':
        cout << "Excellent";
        break;
    case 'B':
        cout << "Good";
        break;
    case 'C':
        cout << "Fair";
        break;
    default:
        cout << "See me";
}

The picture to hold: the body of a switch is one long corridor of statements. Each case label is a numbered door into that corridor. A break is an exit. The switch works out the value in the parentheses, enters through the door with the matching label, and then keeps walking down the corridor, running every statement it passes, until it reaches a break or the closing brace. The labels themselves do nothing. They only mark where the walking can start.

How a switch runs

  1. Work out the expression in the parentheses, here grade.
  2. Look for a case whose value equals it. If one exists, jump there.
  3. If none matches, jump to default. If there is no default, skip the whole switch: nothing runs.
  4. Run statements from that point on, in order, ignoring any other labels passed on the way.
  5. Stop at a break, which leaves the switch, or at the closing brace.
gradeEnters atOutput
'A'case 'A':, runs to its breakExcellent
'C'case 'C':, runs to its breakFair
'F'no match, so default:See me
'a'no match ('a' is not 'A'), so default:See me

The default section is the switch's "none of the above", the same job the trailing else does in an if/else if chain. Python has no classic switch. Its usual tool is an if/elif chain.

Fall-through: what happens without break

Because the switch keeps walking until it meets a break, a missing break lets execution run on into the next case's statements. This is called fall-through.

switch (d)
{
    case 1:
        cout << "one ";       // no break here
    case 2:
        cout << "two ";
        break;
    case 3:
        cout << "three ";
}
dWhat happensOutput
1enters at case 1, falls into case 2, stops at its breakone two
2enters at case 2, stops at the breaktwo
3enters at case 3, reaches the closing bracethree
4no match and no default: skips the switchnothing

Forgetting a break is the most common switch bug. But fall-through is also useful on purpose. Labels can be stacked so that several values share the same code:

switch (answer)
{
    case 'y':
    case 'Y':
        cout << "Yes";      // runs for 'y' or 'Y'
        break;
    case 'n':
    case 'N':
        cout << "No";
        break;
    default:
        cout << "Please type y or n";
}

For 'y' the switch enters at case 'y':, finds no statements there, and walks straight on into the code under case 'Y':. This is the correct way to say "2 or 3": case 2: case 3:.

default can go anywhere. It is usually last, where it needs no break. If it is placed earlier, it follows the same walking rule: after it runs, execution falls into the next case unless there is a break.

switch (k)
{
    default:
        cout << "other ";      // no break
    case 5:
        cout << "five ";
        break;
}

With k = 9 nothing matches, so the switch enters at default, prints other, falls into case 5, prints five, and stops at the break. With k = 5 it enters at case 5 and prints only five. Where default sits never changes when it is chosen: only when no case matches.

The rules for the expression and the labels

  • The expression in the parentheses must be an integer type or a char: int, char, long, short and so on. A double is not allowed, and neither is a string. Both cause a compile error.
  • Each case label must be a constant of an integer type or char: a literal such as 5 or 'y', or a named constant such as const int MAX = 10; used as case MAX:. An ordinary variable is not allowed, and neither is a condition such as case n > 3: or a range. A label matches exactly one value, by equality.
  • Each value can appear only once. Two labels with the same value are a compile error ("duplicate case value"). The compiler does not pick the first one.
  • Each label ends with a colon: case 2:.

The case 2 || 3: trap. It looks like "2 or 3", but a label is a single value. 2 || 3 is a logical expression: 2 is nonzero, so it is true, and true is 1. So the label is really case 1:. If the switch already has a case 1:, the compiler reports a duplicate case value. If it does not, the code compiles but matches only the value 1, never 2 or 3. Stack the labels instead.

switch or if/else if?

A switch can do one thing: compare one integer or char expression for equality with constant values. A chain fits a switch only if it has that shape:

if (code == 1)            switch (code)
    cout << "red";        {
else if (code == 2)           case 1: cout << "red";  break;
    cout << "green";          case 2: cout << "green"; break;
else                          default: cout << "unknown";
    cout << "unknown";    }

Each == test becomes a case with a break, and the final else becomes default. These chains cannot become a switch: ranges such as score >= 90, tests on different variables such as x == 1 then y == 2, tests joined with && or ||, and comparisons of double or string values. Use if/else if for those.

In pseudocode a switch is often written as Select size, then When 1, When 2 or 3 and so on, then Otherwise. Each When becomes a case (stacked labels for "2 or 3"), each When's action ends with a break, and Otherwise becomes default.

A switch with an initialization clause (C++17)

Like an if, a switch may start with a definition and a semicolon: switch (int r = n % 4; r). The definition runs first, so r gets its value, and then the switch matches on the expression after the semicolon. The clause is optional. r can be used anywhere inside the switch, and nowhere after its closing brace.

switch (int r = 23 % 4; r)     // 23 % 4 is 3
{
    case 3:
        cout << "r is " << r;   // prints r is 3
        break;
    default:
        cout << "other";
}
// cout << r;   here would not compile

Blocks and variable scope

A block is a group of statements inside braces { }, such as the body of an if or of main. A variable defined inside a block is a local variable: it belongs to that block. Its scope, the part of the program where its name can be used, runs from the line that defines it to the closing brace of that block. This is called local scope or block scope.

int total = 5;
if (total > 0)
{
    int bonus = 3;          // bonus exists from here...
    total = total + bonus;
}                           // ...to here
cout << total;              // fine: prints 8
cout << bonus;              // compile error: bonus not declared

This is a real difference from Python, where a variable created inside an if can still be used after it. In C++, a variable defined inside braces is gone after the closing brace. If you need it afterwards, define it before the block. Also, a name can be defined only once in the same block: int a = 1; int a = 2; in one block is a compile error.

The same name in an inner block. An inner block may define a variable with the same name as one outside it. That creates a second, separate variable. Inside the inner block the name means the new variable, which hides the outer one. The outer variable is not touched, and it is visible again after the block ends.

int x = 10;
{
    int x = 99;     // a new x; the outer x is hidden
    x = x + 1;      // changes the inner x to 100
    cout << x;      // 100
}
cout << x;          // 10: the outer x was never changed
Lineouter xinner x
int x = 10;10does not exist
int x = 99;10 (hidden)99
x = x + 1;10 (hidden)100
after }10gone

Hiding names like this is legal but confusing, so avoid it in your own code. Expect it on tests.

Variables inside a case. Since the cases of a switch share one block, defining a variable directly under a case label is a problem: a jump to a later label would skip its initialization, and g++ reports "jump to case label". Put braces around that case's statements to give it its own block:

case 1:
{
    int tax = 7;
    cout << tax;
    break;
}

Mistakes students make

  • Forgetting break, so one case runs on into the next.
  • Thinking a switch runs only the matching case. It runs from the matching label down to the first break.
  • Thinking default runs only when it is last, or stops by itself. It is chosen when nothing matches, and it falls through like any case.
  • Switching on a double or a string.
  • Using a variable, a condition or a range as a case label.
  • Writing case 2 || 3:. Stack the labels: case 2: case 3:.
  • Repeating a case value. That is a compile error.
  • Using a variable after the closing brace of the block that defined it.
  • Thinking a change to an inner variable with the same name changes the outer one.

What to remember for the test

  • A switch jumps to the case equal to the expression, or to default, then runs everything after that point until a break or the closing brace.
  • No match and no default: nothing runs.
  • The expression is an integer type or char. Labels are unique integer or char constants.
  • break leaves the switch. Running on without one is fall-through.
  • Only one variable tested with == against constants converts to a switch. The final else becomes default.
  • switch (init; expr) runs the init first. Its variable exists only inside the switch.
  • A local variable's scope runs from its definition to the end of its block.
  • An inner variable with the same name hides the outer one until the block ends, and the outer one keeps its value.
  • For a switch question, find the entry label, then read straight down, crossing labels, until a break.

questions.prompt: Which operator tests whether two values are NOT equal?
questions.explain:
Not equal is written `!=` in C++: an exclamation mark, which means "not", then an equals sign, with no space between them. For example `if (answer != 42)` is true for every value except 42.

The other choices come from other languages or have the characters in the wrong order. `<>` means not equal in some languages, such as SQL, but C++ rejects it. `!==` is JavaScript's not-equal and also fails to compile. `=!` is backwards. C++ would read `a =! b` as `a = !b`, which stores a value in `a` instead of comparing anything.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume it is inside main.)
questions.explain:
Each comparison in parentheses is either true or false, and `cout` prints true as 1 and false as 0.
```
(7 > 2)     true    prints 1
(7 < 2)     false   prints 0
(3 == 3)    true    prints 1
```
Nothing is printed between the three values, so the digits run together: `101`. If you expected `truefalsetrue`, remember that `cout` prints the words only after `boolalpha` has been sent to it.

questions.prompt: The value of the relational expression 9 < 4 is 0.
questions.explain: True. 9 is not less than 4, so the comparison `9 < 4` is false. In C++ a false comparison has the value 0 and a true one has the value 1. That is why `cout << (9 < 4);` prints 0, not the word false.

questions.prompt: Which relational operator means 'greater than or equal to'? Type the operator.
questions.explain: The operator is `>=`: the `>` first, then `=`, with no space between them. It is true when the left value is bigger than the right one or equal to it. For example `if (age >= 18)` is true for 18 and for every age above it. The reversed spelling `=>` is not a C++ operator and causes a compile error. Saying the words in order helps: "greater than" first, then "or equal".

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume it is inside main.)
questions.code:
int x = 10;
cout << (x > 5 > 2) << endl;
questions.explain:
C++ does not chain comparisons the way math or Python does. Both `>` operators are on the same level, so they are worked left to right.
```
x > 5 > 2
(10 > 5) > 2    10 > 5 is true, which is 1
1 > 2           false, which is 0
```
So it prints `0`. The tempting answer is 1, from reading it as "x is greater than 5, and 5 is greater than 2". C++ never compares x with 2. It compares the result of the first test, 1 or 0, with 2, so this expression is false for every value of x.

questions.prompt: What is printed?
choices: big, but only when n is greater than 10
questions.explain:
Look at the semicolon right after `if (n > 10)`. A semicolon on its own is a null statement: a statement that does nothing. An `if` controls only the one statement right after its parentheses, so this `if` controls that empty statement.
```
if (n > 10) ;     3 > 10 is false, so "do nothing" is skipped
cout << "big";    not part of the if, so it always runs
```
The program prints `big`. "Nothing" is what the code would print without the stray semicolon, and "big, but only when n is greater than 10" describes what the programmer meant, not what was written. It is not a compile error: a null statement is legal, which is why this bug is so easy to miss.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?
questions.explain:
The condition has one `=`, so it is an assignment, not a comparison.
```
k = 5      stores 5 in k. The assignment's value is 5
if (5)     5 is not 0, so the condition is true
```
The `if` part runs and the program prints `yes`. The `else` part runs only when the condition is false, so it is skipped. "no" would be right for `if (k == 5)`, which compares 2 with 5. "yes, and k is still 2" is wrong because the assignment changed k to 5. And the code does compile: C++ allows an assignment as a condition, and the compiler at most warns about it.

questions.prompt: In C++, the condition of an if statement is false only when its value is 0.
questions.explain: True. C++ decides a condition with one rule: 0 is false, and every other value is true. That includes negative numbers, so `if (-1)` runs its statement, and so does `if (42)`. A comparison such as `x > 3` fits the same rule, because it produces 1 or 0. This rule is also why `if (k = 5)` is always true: the assignment's value is 5, which is not 0.

questions.prompt: A student writes: if (x =< 5). What is wrong?
choices: Nothing; it compiles and means less than or equal
x must be written after the 5
It needs a semicolon before the parenthesis
=< is not an operator; the correct spelling is <=
questions.explain:
When a relational operator contains an equals sign, the `=` always comes second: `<=` and `>=`. So `=<` is not an operator, the line does not compile, and the fix is `if (x <= 5)`. Saying it aloud helps: "less than, or equal to" puts the `<` first.

The other choices are wrong. Because it does not compile, it cannot mean less than or equal. The order of `x` and `5` is fine, since either side of a comparison can be a variable or a number. And a semicolon has no place in or before a condition, so adding one fixes nothing.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume it is inside main.)
questions.explain:
There are no braces, so the `if` controls only the first `cout`. The indentation of the second line does not change that, because the compiler ignores indentation.
```
score > 50        40 > 50 is false, so "Pass" is skipped
cout "Congrats"   ordinary statement, always runs
cout "End"        ordinary statement, always runs
```
The output is `Congrats` then `End`, each on its own line. To make Congrats depend on the test, both `cout` lines under the `if` would need to be wrapped in braces.

questions.prompt: What does this code print on a typical PC, where double uses the standard IEEE 754 binary format (as it does with g++)? (Assume it is inside main and <cmath> is included.)
questions.explain:
0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 cannot be stored exactly in binary, just as 1/3 cannot be written exactly in decimal. Each stored value is a tiny bit off.
```
a = 0.1 + 0.2       stored as 0.30000000000000004
0.3                 stored as 0.29999999999999999
a == 0.3            every bit must match: false   "different"
fabs(a - 0.3)       about 0.00000000000000006
... < 0.000001      true                          "close"
```
With the space printed between them, the output is `different close`. The first test fails for a difference far too small to matter. The second asks the better question, "are they within a tolerance?", and gets the sensible answer.

questions.prompt: Comparing two computed double values with == is a reliable way to test whether they are equal.
questions.explain: False. A `double` is stored in binary, and most decimal fractions such as 0.1 cannot be stored exactly. Two calculations that should give the same number can end up a tiny amount apart, and `==` reports them as different. For example, `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` is false on a typical PC. The book's advice is to stick to `<` and `>` comparisons with floating-point values. To test for equality, check that the difference is tiny instead: `fabs(a - b) < 0.000001`.

questions.prompt: Which statement sets `bonus` to 50 when `sales` equals 2000, and sets it to 0 otherwise?
questions.explain:
The condition must compare with `==`, and each branch must store with `=`. Only `if (sales == 2000) bonus = 50; else bonus = 0;` does both.

Each wrong version breaks one rule. `if (sales = 2000)` stores 2000 in sales, and 2000 is not zero, so the condition is always true and bonus is always 50. `if (sales == 2000); bonus = 50; else ...` has a semicolon that ends the if, so `bonus = 50;` is ordinary code and the else has no if to join: a compile error. `bonus == 50;` only compares bonus with 50 and throws the answer away, so bonus is never set.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume it is inside main.)
An if statement placed inside another if statement is called a ___ if statement.
questions.explain: The term is nested. A nested if is an if statement placed inside the if part or the else part of another if. The inner one is tested only when the program reaches it. For example, in `if (n > 0) { if (n % 2 == 0) cout << "even"; }`, the even test happens only for positive numbers.

questions.prompt: A semicolon directly after the closing parenthesis of an if condition is a compile error.
questions.explain:
False. `if (x > 5);` compiles. The lone semicolon is a null statement, a statement that does nothing, and it becomes the one statement the if controls. The line after it is then ordinary code that runs every time. No error appears, which is why this bug is easy to miss.

The semicolon leads to a compile error only indirectly: if another statement and then an `else` follow, as in `if (c); x = 1; else x = 2;`, the else has no if to join.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain:
A condition does not have to be a comparison. C++ treats 0 as false and every other value as true. Here `n` is 0, so `if (n)` is false, the if part is skipped, and the else part prints `F`.

"T" would need `n` to be nonzero. "TF" is impossible, because if/else always runs exactly one branch. "Nothing" is impossible too, for the same reason: when the condition is false, the else part runs.

questions.prompt: A flowchart shows a decision diamond 'Is age >= 18?'. The Yes path leads to a second diamond 'Is member?', whose Yes path prints Discount and whose No path prints Regular. The first diamond's No path prints Minor. Which code matches?
choices: if (age >= 18) { if (member) cout << "Discount"; } else cout << "Regular"; else cout << "Minor";
if (age >= 18 && member) cout << "Discount"; else cout << "Regular"; cout << "Minor";
if (age >= 18) { if (member) cout << "Discount"; else cout << "Regular"; } else cout << "Minor";
if (age >= 18) cout << "Discount"; if (member) cout << "Regular"; else cout << "Minor";
questions.explain:
The "member?" question is asked only on the Yes path of the age question, so it must be an if nested inside the if part. It has two exits of its own, so it gets its own else. The first diamond's No exit becomes the outer else. That gives `if (age >= 18) { if (member) cout << "Discount"; else cout << "Regular"; } else cout << "Minor";`.

The others fail. The version with `} else cout << "Regular"; else cout << "Minor";` has two elses for the outer if, and the second has no if to join, so it does not compile. The version using `&&` (and) leaves `cout << "Minor";` outside every if, so Minor prints for everyone, and minors are also told Regular. The version with two separate ifs asks about membership for everyone, so an adult member sees DiscountRegular.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume it is inside main.)
questions.explain:
A chain tests its conditions from the top and stops at the first true one.
```
s >= 60     95 >= 60 is true: print D, leave the chain
s >= 90     never tested
else        skipped
```
So the output is `D`. The tempting answer is A, because 95 is an A score. But the A test comes second, and 95 already passed the first, wider test. To work as intended, the chain must test `s >= 90` before `s >= 60`.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume it is inside main.)
questions.explain:
There are two separate statements here. The first `if (n > 10)` stands alone: it has no else. The second `if (n > 5)` starts a new chain, because it is not preceded by `else`.
```
if (n > 10)        15 > 10 true    print A
if (n > 5)         15 > 5 true     print B, leave the chain
else if (n > 1)    not tested
else               skipped
```
Output: `AB`. Answering only `A` treats the whole thing as one chain. Only `else if` continues a chain, so the second if is tested whatever happened to the first.

questions.prompt: In an if/else if chain, when does the trailing else run?
choices: Whenever the first if is false
Every time, after the other branches
Only when the last else if is true
Only when every condition above it was false
questions.explain:
The trailing else is the chain's "none of the above". It runs only when every condition above it was false. As soon as any condition is true, its branch runs and the program leaves the chain, so the else is skipped.

The wrong choices each miss part of that. If the first if is false, a later else if may still be true and take the branch. The else never runs every time, because a chain runs at most one branch. And when the last else if is true, that branch runs instead of the else.

questions.prompt: In an if/else if chain, once one condition is true, the conditions after it are not evaluated.
questions.explain: True. A chain runs at most one branch. When a condition is true, its branch runs and the program jumps past the end of the whole chain. The later conditions are never tested. For example, with `score = 95` in `if (score >= 90) ... else if (score >= 80) ...`, the test `score >= 80` is never evaluated. Separate if statements are different: each one is tested.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume it is inside main.)
questions.explain:
The part before the semicolon runs first and creates `r`. Then the condition is tested.
```
int r = 17 % 5     17 divided by 5 is 3 remainder 2, so r is 2
r == 2             true
if part            prints "r is " then r, which is 2
```
Output: `r is 2`. The variable made in the initialization clause can be used in the condition, the if part and the else part, so printing it inside the if part is fine.

questions.prompt: In C++17, where can a variable defined in an if statement's initialization clause be used?
choices: Inside the if statement and its else parts only
Anywhere later in the same function
questions.explain:
A variable defined in the initialization clause belongs to that one if statement. It can be used in the condition, in the if part and in every else part, and it disappears when the whole statement ends. Using it on a later line is a compile error.

The other choices are wrong. It is not available later in the function, which is the whole point of the clause: it keeps a helper variable local to one decision. And it is not limited to the condition or to the else branch, since the if part and the else part can both use it.

questions.prompt: A variable, often a bool, that signals whether some condition has occurred is called a ___.
What does this code print? (Assume it is inside main.)
questions.code:
bool ok = (5 < 2);
cout << ok << " " << !ok << endl;
questions.explain:
Work out `ok` first, then its opposite.
```
ok = (5 < 2)     5 is not less than 2: false
cout << ok       false prints as 0
!ok              ! means NOT: not false is true
cout << !ok      true prints as 1
```
With the space between them, the output is `0 1`. `cout` shows a bool as 1 or 0, not as the words, unless `boolalpha` has been sent to it.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
bool b = 25;
cout << b;
questions.explain:
A `bool` can hold only true or false. When a number is stored in one, 0 becomes false and every other number becomes true. So `bool b = 25;` keeps no trace of 25, only that it was nonzero, and `b` is true.

`cout` prints a true bool as `1`. It would print the word `true` only after `boolalpha`, which this code does not use. `25` is wrong because the bool cannot hold 25. `0` is wrong because only zero becomes false.

questions.prompt: Pseudocode: if temp is below 32 show Freezing; otherwise, if temp is below 60 show Cold; otherwise show Warm. Which code is correct?
choices: if (temp < 60) cout << "Cold"; else if (temp < 32) cout << "Freezing"; else cout << "Warm";
if (temp < 32) cout << "Freezing"; if (temp < 60) cout << "Cold"; else cout << "Warm";
if (temp < 32) cout << "Freezing"; else if (temp < 60) cout << "Cold"; else cout << "Warm";
if (temp < 32) cout << "Freezing"; else if (temp > 60) cout << "Cold"; else cout << "Warm";
questions.explain:
The chain must test `temp < 32` first. Only when that is false does it go on to ask `temp < 60`, so Cold covers 32 to 59, and the else gives Warm for 60 and up. That is `if (temp < 32) ... else if (temp < 60) ... else ...`.

Check the others with a value. At 20 degrees, the version that tests `temp < 60` first stops there and shows Cold, so Freezing can never appear. The version with two separate ifs shows both Freezing and Cold for 20, because the second if is tested anyway. The version testing `temp > 60` for Cold shows Warm for 45 and Cold for 75.

questions.prompt: Which C++ data type (give its keyword) is most often used for a flag that holds either true or false?
questions.explain: The keyword is `bool`. A bool variable holds only `true` or `false`, which C++ prints as 1 or 0, so it is the natural type for a flag: `bool found = false;`, later `found = true;`, then `if (found) ...`. Be careful with the spelling. `boolean` is the Java spelling and is not a C++ type.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume it is inside main.)
questions.code:
bool a = true, b = false, c = false;
cout << (a || b && c) << ((a || b) && c) << endl;
questions.explain:
Without parentheses, `&&` groups more tightly than `||`, the way `*` does with `+`. So the first expression means `a || (b && c)`.
```
a || (b && c)     a is true, so || is true at once
                  (b && c) is skipped     prints 1

(a || b) && c     parentheses force this grouping
a || b            true || false is true
true && c         true && false is false  prints 0
```
The output is `10`. Grouping the first expression left to right, as `(a || b) && c`, would give 0, the same as the second. The two differ only because of how they group. Working out `b && c` first gives the same answer: it is false, and `true || false` is still true.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume it is inside main.)
questions.explain:
`&&` works out its left side first, and when that side is false it skips the right side completely.
```
x != 0          0 != 0 is false
&&              left side false: the right side is skipped,
                so (y = 10) never runs
if              condition is false, "in " is not printed
cout << y       y is still 5
```
The output is `5`. The tempting answer is `10`, from assuming the assignment inside the condition always happens. It only happens when the left side of `&&` is true.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume it is inside main.)
questions.explain:
`||` works out its left side first. If that side is true, the answer is already true, so the right side is skipped.
```
n > 1           3 > 1 is true
||              left side true: ++n > 100 is skipped,
                so n is never increased
r               true, prints 1
n               still 3
```
`r` and `n` are printed with nothing between them, so the output is `13`. If you answered `14`, you ran `++n`, which adds 1 to n, but short-circuit evaluation means it never runs here.

questions.prompt: Which condition is true when score is OUTSIDE the range 0 to 100?
questions.explain:
A score is outside 0 to 100 when it is below the low end OR above the high end. Only one of those needs to be true, so the test is `score < 0 || score > 100`.

`score < 0 && score > 100` asks for both at once, and no number is below 0 and above 100, so it is never true. `score >= 0 && score <= 100` is the inside test, the exact reverse. `!(score < 0 || score > 100)` is NOT of the correct outside test, so it is also true only for scores inside the range.

questions.prompt: Which logical operator, written !, reverses the truth value of its operand? Give its name.
questions.explain: The `!` operator is called NOT (logical NOT). It takes one value and flips it: `!true` is false and `!false` is true. For example, `if (!done)` runs when `done` is false. Because `!` is done before comparisons, write `!(x > 5)` to negate a comparison.

questions.prompt: Let p be 1, q be 0 and r be 0. Then the expression `p || q && r` is true.
questions.explain:
True. `&&` groups more tightly than `||`, so the expression means `p || (q && r)`.
```
q && r      0 && 0 is 0 (false)
p || 0      1 || 0 is 1 (true)
```
The result is 1, true. A running program actually checks p first, and since p is true it skips `q && r` completely. The result is the same. The trap is to group left to right as `(p || q) && r`, which gives `1 && 0`, false. Without parentheses, the `&&` always groups with its two neighbours, `q` and `r`.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume it is inside main.)
questions.explain:
`!` is done before `>`, so in the first expression it applies to `x` alone.
```
!x > 5        means (!x) > 5
!x            x is 3, nonzero, so true; !true is false, 0
0 > 5         false                      prints 0

!(x > 5)      parentheses first
x > 5         3 > 5 is false
!false        true                       prints 1
```
The output is `01`. Reading `!x > 5` as "x is not greater than 5" gives 1 for both. To negate a comparison, it must be wrapped in parentheses.

questions.prompt: Which operator has the LOWEST precedence?
questions.explain:
`||` has the lowest precedence of the four. From highest to lowest the order is `!`, then the comparisons (`==` among them), then `&&`, then `||`. That is why `a || b && c` means `a || (b && c)`: `||` binds most loosely, so it joins `a` with the whole of `b && c`.

`!` is the highest of the four, since it applies to the value right next to it. `==` is done before both logical operators, so comparisons are finished before they are joined. `&&` groups before `||`. Assignment, which is not a choice here, is lower still.

questions.prompt: With p true and q false, what is the value of `!(p && q) && (p || q)`? (cout displays a bool value as 1 or 0.)
questions.code:
bool p = true, q = false;
cout << (!(p && q) && (p || q));
questions.explain:
Work it out piece by piece.
```
p && q        true && false is false
!(p && q)     !false is true
p || q        true || false is true
true && true  true, which cout shows as 1
```
So the value is true, shown as 1. Short-circuit evaluation never changes the result, only whether the right side gets evaluated. It does not matter here anyway: the left side is true, so `&&` has to check the right side. And the expression is valid C++: `!` may be applied to a parenthesized expression.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume it is inside main.)
questions.code:
bool p = true, q = false;
cout << (p && q) << (p || q) << (!p) << (!q) << endl;
questions.explain:
Use the truth table row where p is true and q is false.
```
p && q     both must be true: false    prints 0
p || q     one is enough: true         prints 1
!p         not true: false             prints 0
!q         not false: true             prints 1
```
