Nothing is printed between them, so the output is `0101`.

questions.prompt: Which condition is equivalent to !(a > 5 || b < 3)?
questions.explain:
Use De Morgan's law: to move a NOT inside, flip the joining operator and replace each comparison with its opposite.
```
!(a > 5 || b < 3)
flip || to &&:        !(a > 5) && !(b < 3)
opposite of each:     a <= 5 && b >= 3
```
The opposite of `>` is `<=`, and the opposite of `<` is `>=`, because the equal case must move across. `a <= 5 || b >= 3` forgot to flip the operator. `a < 5 && b > 3` got the opposites wrong and wrongly leaves out a = 5 and b = 3. `a > 5 && b < 3` negates nothing.

questions.prompt: A program that tests user input before using it is performing input ___.
questions.explain: The answer is validation. Input validation means checking input before the program uses it, for example `if (age < 0 || age > 120) cout << "Invalid age";`. Without it, bad input produces bad results: garbage in, garbage out.

questions.prompt: A menu program shows choices 1 to 4. After reading choice, which design best handles a value like 9?
choices: Assume the user always types 1 to 4, since the menu lists only those values
Use four separate if statements, one per valid choice, with no else
Put a nested if inside each menu item's branch to check the choice again
End the switch or if/else if chain with a default or final else that reports an invalid choice
questions.explain:
The best design ends the chain or switch with a catch-all, a final `else` or `default`, that reports an invalid choice. Any value not on the menu, such as 9, 0 or -5, lands there.

The other designs fail. Assuming the user always types 1 to 4 ignores typing mistakes, the problem input validation exists to solve. Four separate ifs with no else simply do nothing for 9, so the user gets no message. Re-checking the choice inside each branch is pointless, because those branches only run for valid choices, and 9 never reaches any of them.

questions.prompt: In the expression (d != 0 && total / d > 2), division by zero cannot occur when d is 0.
questions.explain: True. `&&` works out its left side first, and when the left side is false it skips the right side. When d is 0, `d != 0` is false, so `total / d > 2` is never evaluated and no division happens. The whole condition is simply false. This is why the guard goes on the left. Written as `total / d > 2 && d != 0`, the division would happen first.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume it is inside main and the ASCII character set.)
questions.explain:
Characters compare by their ASCII codes, so replace each one with its code.
```
'a' > 'A'     97 > 65     true    1
'9' < 'A'     57 < 65     true    1
'Z' < 'a'     90 < 97     true    1
```
The output is `111`. The third one surprises people, because Z is the last letter. But every uppercase code (65 to 90) is smaller than every lowercase code (97 to 122), so any capital letter is less than any small letter.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume it is inside main and the ASCII character set.)
questions.explain:
Strings are compared one character at a time from the left, by ASCII code, and the first difference decides.
```
s1[0] = 'Z'    code 90
s2[0] = 'a'    code 97
90 < 97        so "Zebra" < "apple"
```
The condition is true, so the output is `Zebra first`. The tempting answer is apple first, from alphabet order. But the comparison is case sensitive, and every uppercase letter has a smaller code than every lowercase letter.

questions.prompt: Which is true of the strings "cat" and "category" (as string objects)?
questions.code:
string a = "cat", b = "category";
cout << (a < b);
questions.explain:
Compare one character at a time: c = c, a = a, t = t. Then "cat" runs out while "category" still has characters left. When one string runs out and all its characters have matched, the shorter string is less. So `"cat" < "category"` is true.

They are not equal, because equal strings must have the same length and every character the same. And string objects can always be compared with the relational operators. That is exactly what dictionary order needs.

questions.prompt: Two string objects with the same letters compare equal with == only if their letter cases also match.
questions.explain: True. `==` on strings checks every character, and an uppercase letter is a different character from its lowercase version, with a different code: 'C' is 67 and 'c' is 99. So `"Cat" == "cat"` is false, while `"cat" == "cat"` is true. To compare without caring about case, a program has to convert both strings to the same case first.

questions.prompt: The ?: operator, which has three operands, is called the ___ operator.
questions.explain: The answer is conditional. `?:` is the conditional operator: `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse`. It is the only C++ operator with three operands, so it is also called the ternary operator. Example: `fee = (age < 12) ? 5 : 10;` stores 5 for a child and 10 for everyone else.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume it is inside main.)
questions.code:
int n = 5;
cout << (n % 2 == 0 ? "even" : "odd") << (n > 3 ? 1 : 0) << endl;
questions.explain:
Work out each conditional operator on its own.
```
n % 2 == 0     5 % 2 is 1, and 1 == 0 is false
? "even" : "odd"   false picks the value after :   "odd"
n > 3          5 > 3 is true
? 1 : 0        true picks the value after ?        1
```
The two results are printed with nothing between them: `odd1`. The parentheses around each `?:` are required. Without them `<<` would grab part of the expression first, and the line would not compile.

questions.prompt: Which statement is equivalent to result = (x > 0) ? 10 : 20; ?
questions.explain:
In `result = (x > 0) ? 10 : 20;` the value right after `?` is used when the condition is true, and the value after `:` when it is false. So it means: if x > 0, result is 10, otherwise result is 20. That is `if (x > 0) result = 10; else result = 20;`.

The version that gives 20 for true has the values swapped. `result = 10; if (x > 0) result = 20;` also swaps them. `if (x > 0) result = 10; result = 20;` has no else, so the second assignment always runs and result always ends up 20.

questions.prompt: What is the value of v after: int x = 4; int v = x > 2 ? x * 2 : x / 2;
questions.explain:
`?:` has very low precedence, so `x > 2` is the whole condition, and `x * 2` and `x / 2` are the two whole values to choose between. Only the chosen one is worked out.
```
x > 2          4 > 2 is true
? x * 2        true picks this value: 4 * 2 is 8
: x / 2        not evaluated
v              8
```
So v is 8. 2 is what the false branch, `x / 2`, would give. 4 is just x, unchanged. 1 might come from thinking the comparison itself is stored, but the comparison only chooses which value is used.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume it is inside main.)
questions.explain:
A switch enters at the matching label and then keeps running every statement below it until it meets a `break`.
```
n is 2         enter at case 2
case 2         print B, no break, keep going
case 3         print C, then break: leave the switch
case 4         never reached
```
The output is `BC`. The tempting answer is `B`, from thinking a switch runs only the matching case. Labels do not stop execution, only `break` does. Case 1 is skipped because execution starts at case 2.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume it is inside main.)
questions.explain:
No label is 9, so the switch enters at `default`. Its position at the top does not matter for choosing it, but once it runs, it falls through like any other case.
```
v is 9         no case 9: enter at default
default        print D, no break, keep going
case 1         print 1, then break: leave the switch
```
The output is `D1`. If you answered `D`, you assumed default stops by itself. Only a `break` or the closing brace ends a switch.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume it is inside main.)
questions.explain:
The initialization clause runs first, then the switch matches on `r`.
```
int r = 17 % 4    17 is 4 * 4 + 1, so r is 1
switch (r)        enter at case 1
case 1            print one, then break
```
The output is `one`. Case 0 does not match, and `default` is used only when no case matches, so many is not printed.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume it is inside main.)
questions.explain:
The braces make a block, and the `int x = 99;` inside it creates a second, separate variable that hides the outer x.
```
int x = 10        outer x is 10
{ int x = 99      inner x is 99, outer is hidden
  cout << x       prints the inner one: 99
}                 inner x is gone
cout << x         outer x, never changed: 10
```
Output: `99 10`. Answering `99 99` treats the inner definition as a change to the outer x. It is a new variable with the same name.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume it is inside main.)
questions.explain:
Inside the braces, `int v = 2;` defines a new variable that hides the outer v. Every use of v in that block means the inner one.
```
outer v = 1
v == 1            true, enter the block
int v = 2         inner v is 2
v += 10           inner v is 12
cout << v         prints 12 and a space
}                 inner v is gone
cout << v         outer v, never touched: 1
```
The output is `12 1`. The outer v stays 1 because `v += 10` changed only the inner variable.

questions.prompt: A switch expression may be a double.
questions.explain: False. The expression in a switch must be an integer type or a char, such as `int`, `char` or `long`. A `double` causes a compile error, and so does a `string`. To choose based on a double, use an if/else if chain.

questions.prompt: What may a case label be?
choices: A relational expression such as x > 5
An integer or char constant such as 5, 'y' or a const int
questions.explain:
A case label must be a constant of an integer type or char: a literal such as `5` or `'y'`, or a named constant such as `const int MAX = 10;`. Each label matches exactly one value, by equality.

An ordinary int variable is not allowed, because its value is not fixed when the program is compiled. A range such as 1 to 10 is not standard C++ (g++ happens to accept `case 1 ... 10:` as its own extension). A condition such as `x > 5` is not a label either. Ranges and conditions need an if/else if chain.

questions.prompt: Which keyword makes control leave a switch statement?
questions.explain:
The keyword is `break`. When a switch reaches a `break`, it leaves the switch and continues with the statement after its closing brace. Without one, execution falls through into the next case's statements:
```
case 1: cout << "one"; break;   // stops here
case 2: cout << "two";          // falls into the next case
```

questions.prompt: What is the term for execution continuing from one case into the next because there is no break?
questions.explain:
The term is fall-through. A switch runs from the matching label until it meets a `break`, so without one it falls through into the next case. Sometimes that is a bug, and sometimes it is deliberate, as with stacked labels `case 'y': case 'Y':`.

The other terms belong elsewhere. Short-circuiting is when `&&` or `||` skips its right side. Hiding is when an inner variable has the same name as an outer one. "Defaulting" is not a C++ term.

questions.prompt: The part of a program in which a variable can be used is its ___.
questions.explain: The answer is scope. A variable's scope is the part of the program where its name can be used. For a variable defined inside a block, that is from the line that defines it to the closing brace of that block. For example, a variable defined inside an if's braces cannot be used after the closing brace.

questions.prompt: What happens with this code?
choices: Compile error: y is not defined at the cout
questions.explain:
`y` is defined inside the braces of the if, so its scope ends at that closing brace. By the time the `cout` runs, the name `y` no longer exists, and the compiler reports that y was not declared in this scope.

So the program never runs at all: it cannot print 5, 0 or a garbage value. Printing 5 would be true in Python, where a variable made inside an if survives after it. In C++, define `y` before the if if it is needed afterwards.

questions.prompt: A switch statement with two case labels having the same value is legal; the first one is used.
questions.explain: False. Each case value may appear only once in a switch. Two labels with the same value make the program fail to compile, with an error such as "duplicate case value". The compiler does not quietly use the first one. This is also why `case 2 || 3:` often fails: `2 || 3` is true, which is 1, so it duplicates any existing `case 1:`.

questions.prompt: Which is true of the variable r in switch (int r = n % 4; r) { ... } ?
choices: r can be used after the closing brace of the switch
The initialization runs after the cases are matched
r can be used only inside the switch statement
A switch cannot have an initialization clause in any version of C++
questions.explain:
`r` is created by the switch's initialization clause, which C++17 allows. Its scope is the switch statement: it can be used in the expression after the semicolon and anywhere inside the switch's braces, and it is gone after the closing brace.

The other claims are wrong. Using r after the closing brace is a compile error. The initialization runs first, before any case is matched, since the switch needs r to know which case to pick. And the clause is valid in C++17 and later, so "not in any version" is false.

questions.prompt: When cout prints a relational expression that is true, what number appears?
questions.explain: A true comparison has the value 1, and `cout` prints that number. In `cout << (6 >= 6);` the test asks whether 6 is greater than or equal to 6. The two are equal, so the answer is true and `1` is printed. A false comparison prints `0`. You would see the word `true` only if `boolalpha` had been sent to `cout` first, as in `cout << boolalpha << (6 >= 6);`.

questions.prompt: An expression such as `total >= limit`, which compares two values with one of the six comparison operators, is called a ___ expression. (Give the book's term.)
questions.explain: The term is relational expression. It is an expression that compares two values with `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=`, `==` or `!=`. The name comes from what it tests: the relationship between the two values, such as which one is bigger or whether they are equal. Its value is always true or false, so it is also called a Boolean expression. In `if (total >= limit)`, the relational expression is `total >= limit`.

questions.prompt: The compiler uses indentation to decide which statements an if statement controls.
questions.explain: False. The compiler ignores indentation completely. Without braces, an if controls exactly one statement: the first one after the condition. Every later line is ordinary code, however far it is indented. To make several statements depend on the condition, put them in braces `{ }`. Programmers still indent the controlled statements, but that is for people reading the code. Python is different, because there indentation is the structure.

questions.prompt: With n equal to -3, this code still prints B, although the programmer wanted both lines to happen only when n is positive. What pair of symbols must be placed around the two `cout` lines to fix it?
In a switch, the `default:` section runs when no case label matches. Which clause of an if/else if chain plays that same catch-all role?
questions.explain: The answer is the trailing else, the final `else` with no condition at the end of the chain. It runs only when every condition above it was false, so it handles "none of the above", often with an error message. A switch's `default:` section does the same job when no case label matches.

questions.prompt: Any if/else if chain could be rewritten as nested if/else statements, because each else if is simply an if statement placed in the else part of the one before it.
questions.explain:
True. `else if` is not a special keyword. It is an `else` whose single statement is another `if`. So
```
if (a) X; else if (b) Y; else Z;
```
means exactly
```
if (a) X; else { if (b) Y; else Z; }
```
Any chain can be rewritten this way, one level of nesting for each `else if`. The chain form is used because it is easier to read and does not keep moving to the right.

questions.prompt: In the code below, the statement `cout << "X";` is reached only when a is false and b is true.
questions.explain:
True. Follow the two roads. If `a` is true, the if part runs, P is printed, and the else part, with everything inside it, is skipped. So X can never be reached when a is true.

If `a` is false, the program enters the else part and meets the inner test `if (b)`. X prints only if `b` is true there. So X is reached only when a is false and b is true.

questions.prompt: A local int variable that is defined without an initial value, such as `int count;` inside main, automatically starts at 0.
questions.explain: False. A local variable, one defined inside a function such as `main`, does not start at 0 when it is not given a value. It holds whatever happened to be left in that piece of memory, a garbage value, and a program that reads it is wrong and may behave differently from run to run. That is why a flag or counter should get its starting value when it is defined: `int count = 0;` or `bool found = false;`.

questions.prompt: This test is meant to be true only when `age` is in the range 13 through 19. What is wrong with it?
questions.code:
if (age >= 13 || age <= 19)
    cout << "Teen";
choices: It is true only when age is exactly 13 or exactly 19
Nothing; || is the right operator for testing whether a value is inside a range
It is true for every value of age; the two tests must be joined with && instead
It is never true, because no age can pass both tests
questions.explain:
It is true for every age. With `||`, passing either test is enough, and every number passes at least one of them.
```
age 5     5 >= 13 false, 5 <= 19 true       true
age 16    true, true                         true
age 40    40 >= 13 true                      true
```
A value inside a range must pass both limits, so the tests must be joined with `&&`: `age >= 13 && age <= 19`. `||` is the right operator for an outside test. The code is not limited to exactly 13 or 19: it accepts every age. And "never true" describes a different mistake, `age < 13 && age > 19`, which no number can pass.

questions.prompt: `paid` is a bool flag. Which statement sets `fee` to 0 only when the flag is set (true)?
questions.explain:
A bool can be the whole condition. `if (paid)` runs its statement when `paid` is true, which is exactly "only when the flag is set".

The others are wrong. `if (paid = true)` uses one `=`, so it stores true in `paid` and is then true every time: fee becomes 0 even for someone who has not paid. `if (!paid)` uses NOT, so it runs when the flag is NOT set, the reverse of what is wanted. `if (paid == 0)` is the same reverse test, because false is 0.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume it is inside main.)
questions.explain:
Do the arithmetic first, then the size comparisons (`<`, `>`), and only then `==`.
```
a * 2 > b       8 > 9           false   0
b - a == 5      5 == 5          true    1
3 == 2 < 1      2 < 1 first     false   0
                then 3 == 0     false   0
```
The three values print with nothing between them: `010`. The last one is the trap. Working left to right you would do `3 == 2` (0) and then `0 < 1` (1), and answer `011`. But `<` comes before `==` in precedence, so `2 < 1` is worked out first, and its result, 0, is what gets compared with 3.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume it is inside main and the ASCII character set.)
questions.explain:
The character `'7'` and the number `7` are different values. A char stores its ASCII code, and the code of `'7'` is 55.
```
'7' == 7          55 == 7         false   0
'7' == 55         55 == 55        true    1
'7' - '0' == 7    55 - 48 is 7,
                  then 7 == 7     true    1
```
The output is `011`. Subtracting `'0'` works because the digit codes run in order from 48, so any digit character minus `'0'` gives the number it shows.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? (Assume it is inside main, <string> is included, and the ASCII character set.)
questions.explain:
Strings are compared as text, one character at a time, never as numbers.
```
a[0] = '1'     code 49
b[0] = '2'     code 50
49 < 50        decided at once: "100" < "25"
```
So `a < b` is true and the program prints `100 comes first`. The tempting answer is `25 comes first`, because 25 is the smaller number. But the comparison stops at the first characters that differ and never considers how many digits each string has.

questions.prompt: Which of these if/else if chains could be rewritten directly as a switch statement?
choices: if (code == 1) ... else if (code == 2) ... else if (code == 5) ... else ...
questions.explain:
A switch can only compare one integer or char expression for equality with constant values. The chain on `code` does exactly that: `code == 1`, `code == 2`, `code == 5`. Each test becomes a case and the final else becomes `default`.

The others cannot be converted. `score >= 90` and `score >= 80` are ranges, and a label matches one value. `x == 1` then `y == 2` tests two different variables, but a switch tests one expression. `price == 9.5` compares a double, and a switch expression cannot be a double.

questions.prompt: Pseudocode: Select on size. When 1, display S. When 2 or 3, display M. Otherwise display L. Which C++ matches it for every value of size?
choices: switch (size) { case 1: cout << "S"; case 2: case 3: cout << "M"; break; default: cout << "L"; }
switch (size) { case 1: cout << "S"; break; case 2: case 3: cout << "M"; break; default: cout << "L"; }
switch (size) { case 1: cout << "S"; break; case 2 || 3: cout << "M"; break; default: cout << "L"; }
switch (size) { case 1: cout << "S"; break; case 2: case 3: cout << "M"; break; }
questions.explain:
The pseudocode needs three things: a break after S, stacked labels for "2 or 3", and a default for everything else. Only `case 1: cout << "S"; break; case 2: case 3: cout << "M"; break; default: cout << "L";` has all three.

Each other version misses one. Without the break after case 1, size 1 falls through and prints SM. `case 2 || 3:` is really `case 1:`, because `2 || 3` is true, which is 1. That duplicates case 1, so it does not compile. The version with no default prints nothing for a size such as 7 instead of L.

questions.prompt: What does this code print if the user types 14? (Assume it is inside main.)
questions.explain:
Trace from the outside in with n = 14, and watch the braces.
```
n > 0       14 > 0 true    print P, enter the block
n > 10      14 > 10 true   print Q, enter its block
n > 20      14 > 20 false  R is skipped
else S      belongs to if (n > 10), which was true: skipped
```
The output is `PQ`. The tempting mistake is to pair the `else` with `if (n > 20)`, the nearest if, and print S. But `if (n > 20)` is inside the braces that close just before the else. An else cannot reach inside a closed block, so it belongs to `if (n > 10)`.

questions.prompt: For int variables p and q, the expression `p < q` always has the same value as `q >= p`.
questions.explain:
False. Try the case where the two values are equal, say p = 4 and q = 4.
```
p < q      4 < 4      false
q >= p     4 >= 4     true
```
They disagree, so they are not always the same. `q >= p` allows equality and `p < q` does not. Swapping the sides of `p < q` correctly gives `q > p`, with no "or equal". The opposite of `p < q` is `p >= q`.

questions.prompt: Assume `int i = 3, j = 8, k = 0;`. Which condition is FALSE?
questions.explain:
Work out each choice with i = 3, j = 8, k = 0.
```
i == 3 || j < 2      true || false      true
j > i && k == 0      true && true       true
k != 0 || i > j      false || false     false
!(i > j)             !(3 > 8) = !false  true
```
So the false one is `k != 0 || i > j`. `||` is false only when both sides are false, and here k is 0 and 3 is not greater than 8.

questions.prompt: Which statement sets `fee` to 5 when `age` is under 12 and to 10 otherwise?
questions.explain:
The form is `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse`. The condition is `age < 12`. The value for true, 5, goes right after the `?`, and the value for false, 10, goes after the `:`. That is `fee = (age < 12) ? 5 : 10;`.

`fee = (age < 12) ? 10 : 5;` compiles but has the values swapped, so children pay 10. `: 5 ? 10` puts the symbols in the wrong order, and `? 5, 10` uses a comma where the `:` must go. Neither of those compiles.

questions.prompt: What happens with this code?
choices: It does not compile: without braces the if ends after its first statement, so the else has no matching if
When qty is 0 it prints None left. Reorder now. and otherwise it prints In stock.
It prints Reorder now. every time, followed by In stock. when qty is not 0
It compiles, and the else pairs with the second cout statement
questions.explain:
It does not compile. Indentation does not make a block. Without braces the if controls only `cout << "None left. ";`, and the if statement ends there. `cout << "Reorder now.";` is a separate, ordinary statement. An else must come straight after the statement its if controls. This one comes after an unrelated statement, so it has no if to join, and g++ reports "else without a previous if".

That rules out every choice that describes output, because the program never runs. The choice saying the else pairs with the second cout is wrong too: an else can pair only with an if. Braces around the two cout lines would make it compile.

questions.prompt: Several conditions test the same variable. What is the key difference between writing them as an if/else if chain and as a series of separate if statements?
choices: In the series, testing stops at the first true condition; in the chain, every condition is tested and several branches can run
There is no difference in what runs; the chain is only a shorter way to write the series
The chain can test at most two conditions, while the series can test any number of them
In the chain, testing stops at the first true condition and at most one branch runs; in the series, every if is tested and several can run
questions.explain:
In a chain, conditions are tested from the top and the first true one wins. Its branch runs and the program leaves the chain, so at most one branch runs. A series of separate ifs has no such link. Every if is tested, so a value that passes several tests runs several branches. With a score of 95, separate tests for `>= 90`, `>= 80` and `>= 70` all run, while a chain stops after the first.

The wrong choices reverse the two, claim there is no difference (there is, whenever more than one condition is true), or invent a limit of two conditions (a chain can have any number).

questions.prompt: Trace this pseudocode. What number is displayed?
questions.code:
Set fee to 20
Set weight to 7
If weight > 10 Then
    Add 15 to fee
Else If weight > 5 Then
    Add 8 to fee
Else
    Add 3 to fee
End If
Display fee
questions.explain:
Trace it like C++: test from the top and take only the first true branch.
```
fee = 20, weight = 7
weight > 10 ?    7 > 10 false, go to the next test
weight > 5 ?     7 > 5 true: add 8 to fee, fee is 28
Else             skipped, jump to End If
Display fee      28
```
The answer is `28`. A common slip is to add 3 as well, from the Else. The Else runs only when every test above it is false, and one was true here.

questions.prompt: A flowchart: Start. A process box sets x to 4 and y to 9. A decision diamond asks 'x > y?': the Yes path sets big to x, the No path sets big to y, and the paths rejoin. A second diamond asks 'big % 2 == 0?': Yes displays even, No displays odd. End. What word is displayed?
questions.explain:
Trace it with the values, one diamond at a time.
```
x = 4, y = 9
x > y ?          4 > 9 is false: take No
big = y          big is 9
big % 2 == 0 ?   9 % 2 is 1, and 1 == 0 is false: take No
display odd
```
The word displayed is `odd`. The trap is to think of 4, which is even. The first diamond picked the larger value, 9, and `%` gives the remainder after division, so 9 % 2 is 1, which means odd.

questions.prompt: Which flowchart description matches this code?
choices: One diamond, temp > 100?. Yes displays Hot; No sets fanOn to true; both paths then display Done.
One diamond, temp > 100?. Yes displays Hot, sets fanOn to true and displays Done; No goes straight to End.
One diamond, temp > 100?. Yes goes through two boxes (display Hot, set fanOn to true) and rejoins No; Done is displayed after the paths meet.
Two diamonds in a row, temp > 100? and fanOn?, each with its own display box.
questions.explain:
Turn the code into a chart piece by piece. `if (temp > 100)` is one diamond. The braces put two statements on its Yes path, so that path has two boxes: display Hot, then set fanOn to true. There is no else, so the No path has no boxes. `cout << "Done";` comes after the whole if, so it sits where the two paths join and runs either way.

That matches the description with two boxes on Yes and Done after the join. Setting fanOn on the No path would need an else. Putting Done only on the Yes path would mean it was inside the braces. And there is only one diamond, because the code asks only one question.

questions.prompt: Pseudocode: If qty is at least 1 and at most 50 Then display OK, Else display Invalid. Which C++ matches it?
questions.expect:
Invalid OK OK Invalid
OK OK OK OK
OK OK OK OK
questions.explain:
"At least 1" is `qty >= 1` and "at most 50" is `qty <= 50`. Both must hold, so they are joined with `&&`: `if (qty >= 1 && qty <= 50)`.

The others fail. The `||` version is true for every qty, since every number is at least 1 or at most 50. `1 <= qty <= 50` is not a range test in C++: it compares `1 <= qty` (0 or 1) with 50, so it is always true. The `>` and `<` version drops the end values and calls 1 and 50 Invalid.

questions.prompt: A variable defined inside a block, such as the body of an if, has ___ scope: it can be used only from its definition to the end of that block.
questions.explain: The answer is local (also called block scope). A variable defined inside a block, such as the braces of an if, is local to that block. It can be used from the line that defines it to the block's closing brace, and nowhere else. Example: in `if (x > 0) { int y = 5; }`, `y` cannot be used after the `}`.

questions.prompt: In `a < b || c == d || e > f`, the two || operators are applied in which direction? (The && and || operators share this associativity.)
questions.explain: The answer is left to right. Associativity is the direction in which operators of the same level are grouped. `&&` and `||` group left to right, so `a < b || c == d || e > f` means `(a < b || c == d) || e > f`. Separately, `||` and `&&` always evaluate their left side first, so this one is checked from the left, and as soon as one comparison is true the rest are skipped. The `!` operator is the exception: it groups right to left, so `!!x` means `!(!x)`.

questions.prompt: In C++17, an if statement may include an initialization clause before its condition, but the clause is optional.
questions.explain: True. Since C++17 an if can start with a definition, then a semicolon, then the condition, as in `if (int r = n % 5; r == 2)`. The clause is optional. A plain `if (condition)` is still legal and is still the usual form. The clause just lets a helper variable be created for that one if statement and its else parts. A `switch` can have the same optional clause.

questions.prompt: What does this code print if the user types 0? (Assume it is inside main.)
questions.explain:
The menu line prints first, then the chain checks the input.
```
cout menu        Menu: 1=Add 2=List 3=Quit, then a newline
choice           0
0 < 1 || ...     0 < 1 is true, so || is true at once
                 prints Invalid choice, leaves the chain
```
The output is the menu line, then `Invalid choice` on the next line. Putting the invalid-input test first, as an outside-the-range test with `||`, means the later branches only ever see valid choices.

questions.prompt: Which condition is true exactly when the char variable `ch` holds a digit character, '0' through '9'?
questions.explain:
The digit characters '0' to '9' have the codes 48 to 57, in order. So "ch is a digit" is a range test, and the limits must be the characters, in quotes: `ch >= '0' && ch <= '9'`.

`ch >= 0 && ch <= 9` has no quotes, so it tests the codes 0 to 9. Those are invisible control characters, and no real digit passes. `ch >= '0' || ch <= '9'` is true for every character, because each one is either at least 48 or at most 57. `'0' <= ch <= '9'` is a chained comparison: it compares the 0 or 1 from the first test with 57, so it is always true.

programs.task: Read an integer test score. If it is below 0 or above 100, print 'Invalid score' and stop. Otherwise print 'Grade: ' followed by A for 90 and up, B for 80 to 89, C for 70 to 79, D for 60 to 69, and F below 60. Use an if/else if chain.

programs.task: Show a menu: 1 = circle area, 2 = rectangle area, 3 = quit. Read the choice. For 1 read a radius and print the area (use 3.14159); for 2 read length and width and print the area; for 3 print 'Goodbye'; anything else prints 'Invalid choice'. Use a switch, and print areas with two decimal places. Input here is choice 2, then 4.5 and 3.

programs.task: Read a year. A year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, except that years divisible by 100 are not leap years unless they are also divisible by 400. Print '<year> is a leap year' or '<year> is not a leap year', using logical operators in one condition. Input: 2100.
programs.sampleOutput: Year: 2100 is not a leap year

programs.task: Read two words (strings). Print them on one line separated by a space, in ASCII order (the smaller first). If they are identical print 'Same word'.
